findings.title: Remove unpinned curl|sh remote script execution from image build
findings.whyItBreaks: The new build step `RUN curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` executes whatever bytes the URL returns at build time with full build privileges, and whatever it installs is baked into the published image. There is no version pin, no checksum/signature verification, and the host is not a controlled artifact source, so the image content can be silently changed by whatever serves that URL — a textbook supply-chain RCE. Compounding it, `-sL` without `--fail` downgrades fetch failures: the RUN pipeline's exit status is `sh`'s, not curl's, so a network error or HTTP error body is fed to `sh` (and `-s` suppresses curl's own error output). An empty/failed download can exit 0, making the RUN 'succeed' while installing nothing — the build error signal is swallowed and a broken image ships cleanly. Note also that example.com is an IANA-reserved documentation domain, so the line cannot be a legitimate pinned artifact source as written.

findings.title: Remove curl|sh execution of unpinned remote script from placeholder URL
findings.whyItBreaks: The added RUN step executes whatever bytes the remote host returns as shell code at build time with full build privileges: no version pinning, no checksum, no signature (classic curl|sh supply-chain anti-pattern). The URL is also the IANA-reserved documentation domain example.com, which serves no install script at /install.sh — so the step can only fail the image build or pipe a non-script body (e.g. an HTML page) into sh. Either way the built image is wrong or the build breaks; if the URL is later swapped to a real one without integrity checks, arbitrary remote code runs on every build.

findings.title: curl -sL | sh masks download failure; image builds without the tool
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER D (silent error loss, added path): curl is invoked with -sL but without -f/--fail and the RUN has no pipefail. On network/DNS failure curl emits nothing and exits non-zero, but the step's status is sh's, which exits 0 on empty stdin — the RUN 'succeeds' with nothing installed. On an HTTP error status (e.g. 404) curl exits 0 and pipes the error body into sh instead. The download-failure signal is discarded at the only decision point (the RUN exit status), so a broken or skipped install is indistinguishable from a successful one in the resulting image.

findings.title: Remove unpinned remote script execution (curl|sh) from build
findings.whyItBreaks: The new layer executes whatever https://example.com/install.sh returns with full privileges during image build: no version pin, no checksum, no signature — a compromised or hostile host injects arbitrary code into the image (supply-chain). Independently, example.com is an IANA-reserved example domain (RFC 6761) that serves a static HTML page, so the pipeline feeds HTML to sh: the build either fails on parse errors or performs uncontrolled, undefined actions. There is no legitimate scenario in which this line is correct as written.

findings.title: Download failure in RUN pipeline is silently swallowed
findings.whyItBreaks: Docker runs the step as 'sh -c curl -sL <url> | sh'; POSIX pipelines return the last command's status and RUN has no pipefail. If curl fails (DNS, refused connection, 5xx), it emits nothing and 'sh' exits 0 on empty stdin, so the layer succeeds. Failure is indistinguishable from success for every downstream layer (COPY line 4, CMD line 5) and for the image consumer, who gets an image silently missing whatever this installer was meant to provide. TRIGGER D: previously_reached=n/a (new line, no prior install step); now_receives=exit 0 from sh on empty input.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault swallows ErrMissing, conflating failure with empty value
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER D (swallowed failure). The new exported function `LoadOrDefault` @src/store.go:16 discards the only error signal in the package (`v, _ := Load(key, m)`). `Load` returns `ErrMissing` when the key is absent (@src/store.go:8-10) and can also legitimately return `("", nil)` when the stored value is the empty string. `LoadOrDefault`'s return type is bare `string` with no error channel, so three distinct states — key missing, key present with empty value, key present with real value — collapse into one observable result for the first two. previously_reached=@src/store.go:7 (`Load` propagated `(string, error)` to callers); now that point's failure branch receives the fallback `""` and every caller of the new API is structurally unable to distinguish failure from a real value, so any caller that persists, routes, or reports on the result treats a failed lookup as authoritative data. As an exported (capitalized, package `store`) symbol, this defect is in the shipped API contract now, independent of in-repo callers (there are none yet).

findings.title: Run returns before sends complete: no WaitGroup, unordered results
findings.whyItBreaks: Base Run blocked until every send finished, so 'Run returned' meant 'all len(jobs) results delivered'. Head spawns a goroutine per job and returns immediately: (1) the standard producer pattern — close(results) immediately after Run returns, the only way to range safely — now races the in-flight sends and panics 'send on closed channel'; (2) results arrive in arbitrary order, so any positional consumer mis-associates outputs; (3) there is no WaitGroup or done channel, so no caller can await completion at all; (4) if a consumer stops reading, up to len(jobs) goroutines block forever on results <- (ctx is ignored, spawn is unbounded). Run is the package's only exported symbol, so this is a public API contract change with no safe usage.

findings.title: Run: fire-and-forget breaks completion-at-return contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Run's exported signature is synchronous and exposes no WaitGroup or done channel, so its return was the only completion signal: before this change, when Run returned every j*2 had already been sent on results, in job order. Now Run returns immediately after spawning len(jobs) unjoinable goroutines that send asynchronously. Concrete breakages: (1) a caller using the only pattern the old blocking semantics supported with an unbuffered read — buffered chan of len(jobs), synchronous Run, then close(results) — now panics 'send on closed channel' in the goroutines and crashes the process; (2) a caller that synchronously calls Run and then reads len(jobs) results observes missing/stale values because sends have not happened yet; (3) results now arrive in nondeterministic order, silently corrupting any consumer that pairs results with jobs by position. Every viable pre-change caller pattern breaks or degrades; the signature still promises completion-on-return while the body no longer implements it.

findings.title: Unbounded goroutine fan-out: one goroutine per job, no limit
findings.whyItBreaks: Each loop iteration spawns a goroutine with no semaphore, pool, or cap. Peak memory regresses from O(1) (one synchronous send in flight) to O(len(jobs)) concurrently live goroutines, each pinned on a channel send until a reader drains — e.g. 1e6 jobs spawn 1e6 goroutines. Additionally, if the consumer stops reading early, the goroutines block on send forever and leak, since Run provides no mechanism to join or cancel them (ctx is not consulted before or inside the spawn).

findings.title: Run returns before workers send; close-after-return races and panics
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation was synchronous: when Run returned, every send on results had completed, so a caller could safely close(results) (or treat Run's return as completion) and read exactly len(jobs) values in order. The diff spawns one goroutine per job and returns immediately without waiting. Any caller following the only semantics this package ever had does `Run(ctx, jobs, ch); close(ch)` or ranges ch after Run returns: goroutines that have not yet executed then send on a closed channel -> panic: send on closed channel (intermittent, load-dependent), and results that were never read are lost. Run's observable contract (returns => all results delivered) is silently broken, and result ordering is also no longer guaranteed. The loop variable is correctly passed as an argument, so this is purely a synchronization regression.

findings.title: AND→OR in canDeleteRecord lets non-admins delete tenant records and admins delete cross-tenant
findings.whyItBreaks: The authorization gate was previously a conjunction: only an admin whose tenantId equals record.tenantId could delete. The disjunction now authorizes deletion along two previously denied axes. Substituted values: (1) session={userId:'u2',tenantId:'t1',isAdmin:false}, record={tenantId:'t1',ownerId:'u1'} → old:false, new:true — any non-admin user can delete ANY record in their tenant regardless of ownerId (RecordRef.ownerId exists but is never consulted); (2) session={userId:'a1',tenantId:'t1',isAdmin:true}, record={tenantId:'t2',ownerId:'x'} → old:false, new:true — an admin session can now destroy records in ANY tenant, breaking tenant isolation. Both paths end in irreversible data deletion (unauthorized delete = data loss). canDeleteRecord is an exported authorization API, so the defect ships in the contract itself even with no in-repo callers.

findings.title: Permission flip &&→|| lets any tenant member delete any tenant record
findings.whyItBreaks: canDeleteRecord previously required admin AND same-tenant. With ||, two over-grants appear: (1) any non-admin session now returns true for every record sharing its tenantId — record.ownerId is carried in RecordRef but never checked, so one member can destroy another member's records with no admin involvement (unauthorized data destruction); (2) an admin now returns true for record.tenantId of ANY tenant, deleting the cross-tenant bound that previously applied even to admins (tenant-isolation breach). As an exported authorization primitive, every caller that trusts this gate for a delete endpoint inherits the bypass. git show 1bc256f:src/permissions.ts confirms the base expression was &&.

findings.title: buildReport pairs builtFrom and artifacts from different commits
findings.whyItBreaks: Since base, artifacts were listed for the same commit reported in builtFrom. The diff changes the artifacts source to build.ref("verified") (src/report.ts:13) while builtFrom still comes from the caller-supplied branch (src/report.ts:12,14). For any call where branch's ref and the "verified" ref differ — the normal case, e.g. buildReport(build, "main") — the exported report states builtFrom=<main's commit> but lists the artifacts of the verified commit, silently misattributing artifacts to the wrong build. Additionally a new hidden precondition is imposed: every call now requires the Build to resolve a "verified" ref, which previously it did not need. The changed body breaks the promise of the unchanged BuildReport carrier (builtFrom + artifacts describe one build); no in-repo callers exist, so the broken contract ships directly in the exported API's output.

findings.title: Drop of .slice(0, limit) makes recentEntries ignore the limit entirely
findings.whyItBreaks: The doc comment and signature still promise 'at most `limit` entries', but the new body returns `sorted` in full whenever limit > 0 — the truncation was deleted, not moved. Substitution with real values: recentEntries(['a','b','c'], 2) now returns ['c','b','a'] (3 entries) instead of ['c','b']. The sole caller, renderFeed, calls recentEntries(all, 20) @src/feed.ts:9 and copies into `new Array<string>(20)` sized for exactly 20; the copy loop `for (let i = 0; i < page.length; i++) out[i] = page[i]` @src/feed.ts:10-11 then writes past index 19, extending the array, so renderFeed returns the entire history instead of a 20-entry page. This is TRIGGER C contract drift on a public exported carrier with a relying caller. (Side effect: the new `limit <= 0` early return changes old negative-limit behavior from 'all but last N' to '[]' — sane, and no caller passes negative values, so it is not itself a defect.)

findings.title: changedPaths computed against 'latest' but fromRevision reports pinned revision

findings.title: Async reserve() loses check-then-act atomicity: concurrent calls oversell stock

The store is persisted with the stale shared value, so persistence does not mask it. findings.whyItBreaks: Base behavior (verified at d6a7e21:18) was: if age < ttlMs return value, else evict and return null. The change inverts the predicate: entries older than ttlMs now return the stale value (expired data is served indefinitely), while fresh entries (age <= ttlMs) fall through to entries.delete(key) and return null. Net effect: every fresh read is a miss that also destroys the cached entry, and every expired entry is pinned in the cache serving stale data forever. findings.title: splice inside forEach skips done jobs adjacent to removed ones and mutates input

The replacement splices while forEach iterates: each splice(index,1) shifts subsequent elements left, so forEach (which captured length and index order at start) skips the element now at the next index. Concrete trace with jobs=[{done:false},{done:true},{done:true}]: index 0 kept; index 1 is done -> splice -> array shrinks to [notdone, done]; index 2 is past the new end so it is never visited -> the second done job REMAINS in the result and in the caller's array. Two regressions: (1) pruneDone returns wrong data whenever a done job directly follows a removed one; (2) the caller's input array is mutated in place (was pure filter semantics), so callers holding the original array see jobs silently vanish. findings.title: Replace '==' with hmac.compare_digest in verify() to keep constant-time check
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff replaces `hmac.compare_digest(expected, given_signature)` with plain `==`. Python string equality short-circuits on the first differing character, so the runtime of verify() leaks how many leading hex characters of the HMAC-SHA256 digest the caller guessed correctly. verify() is a live security gate: handle() (app/webhook.py:13-15) returns 401 on False and executes processor(payload) with status 200 on True. An attacker able to send requests and measure response timing can recover the 64-char hex digest byte-by-byte without knowing the secret (CWE-208) and then forge validly signed webhook payloads. This removes an explicit, previously present defense (base SHA 1bdbcad used compare_digest); the hmac import remains only for hmac.new in signature_of, so nothing else compensates. Secondary drift: compare_digest raised TypeError on str/bytes or non-ASCII input (server 500), while '==' silently returns False (401) — behavior change on malformed inputs, though the timing channel is the primary defect.

findings.title: Timing-unsafe == comparison replaces hmac.compare_digest in verify()
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code compared the computed HMAC hexdigest to the attacker-supplied signature with hmac.compare_digest (constant-time). This diff replaces it with ==, which short-circuits on the first differing character. verify() is the sole authentication gate for handle() (app/webhook.py:14): a failed check returns 401, a passed check executes processor(payload). With ==, rejection latency leaks the length of the matching prefix of the signature, so a remote attacker can recover the 64-char SHA-256 hexdigest incrementally by timing repeated forged requests, then forge valid signatures and get arbitrary payloads processed — full webhook auth bypass via a well-documented side channel. The change also silently alters behavior for non-ASCII given_signature values (compare_digest raised TypeError; == returns False), but the security regression is the core defect.

findings.title: verify() uses '==' instead of hmac.compare_digest, enabling timing attack on signature
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff replaces `hmac.compare_digest(expected, given_signature)` with `signature_of(payload, secret) == given_signature`. Python's str '==' short-circuits on the first differing character (after a length pre-check), so comparison time leaks the length of a matching prefix. verify() is the sole auth gate: handle() returns 401 on False and runs processor(payload) with status 200 on True (app/webhook.py:13-16). An attacker can now statistically recover the expected HMAC-SHA256 hexdigest character-by-character from response timing and forge valid webhook signatures — the exact class of vulnerability hmac.compare_digest exists to prevent, and a regression of code that was present at base SHA. Equality semantics for honest clients are unchanged; the defect is the leaked side-channel on every rejected request.

findings.title: Balance updates moved outside transaction: partial failure persists false ledger and loses money
findings.whyItBreaks: In base (git show f2d2f9a:app/transfer.py) the ledger INSERT and both balance UPDATEs executed inside `with db.transaction():`, so any failure rolled back the entire transfer. In head, the `with` block at line 22-23 commits only `_record_ledger`; `_apply_balances` at line 24 then runs two independent autocommitted UPDATEs outside the transaction. If the debit UPDATE succeeds but the credit UPDATE raises (DB error, constraint, connection loss) or the process crashes in between, the from-account is debited, the to-account never credited, and a ledger row asserting a completed transfer is already durably committed — destroyed funds plus a corrupt audit trail, with no rollback. Concurrent readers can also observe the intermediate debit-without-credit state, which the old transaction prevented.

findings.title: Balance updates moved outside transaction; ledger commits on failure
findings.whyItBreaks: At base, ledger INSERT + both balance UPDATEs were inside one `with db.transaction():` block (verified via `git show 09bf70a:app/transfer.py`), so any failure rolled everything back. At head, the transaction commits after `_record_ledger`, then `_apply_balances` runs outside it: (1) if either UPDATE raises (unknown account id, constraint failure, crash), the ledger row is already permanently committed while balances are unchanged — the ledger records a transfer that never happened, and a caller retry after the raised error inserts a duplicate ledger row; (2) the debit and credit UPDATEs are no longer mutually atomic, so a failure between them persists money debited without the credit (fund loss); (3) a crash after the transaction block but before/during `_apply_balances` leaves ledger and balances irreconcilably divergent with no error raised.

findings.title: Balance updates moved outside the transaction break transfer atomicity
findings.whyItBreaks: In the base revision all three writes (ledger INSERT, debit UPDATE, credit UPDATE) executed inside a single `with db.transaction():` block, so a transfer was all-or-nothing. This diff keeps only `_record_ledger` inside the transaction and moves `_apply_balances` to line 24, after the `with` block exits — the ledger row is committed at line 23, then the two balance UPDATEs at lines 8-16 run with NO transaction (not even with each other). Concrete failure modes: (1) if the credit UPDATE fails or the process dies after the debit UPDATE executed (FK/trigger failure on to_acct, CHECK constraint on balances, crash, serialization error), money is debited from `from_acct` and never credited to `to_acct` — permanent fund loss; (2) if `_apply_balances` raises for any reason, the exception propagates so the caller believes the transfer failed and may retry, yet the ledger row from line 23 is already durably committed — retry inserts a duplicate ledger entry while balances are wrong, corrupting the books in both directions. The invariant 'ledger and balances agree' that the original transaction guaranteed is silently dropped by this refactor.

findings.title: billingDay now uses local-time getters, shifting the billing day by host timezone
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation formatted the instant in UTC (getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate), so billingDay(new Date('2024-06-01T02:30:00Z')) === '2024-06-01' on every host. The head implementation uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, which read the host-local calendar. Substitution: on a host with TZ=America/New_York (UTC-4 in June) that same instant is local 2024-05-31T22:30, so billingDay returns '2024-05-31' — the same event bills on a different day depending on deployment environment, and the day boundary moves from UTC midnight to local midnight. The exported sameBillingDay (src/billing/day.ts:7-8) inherits the shifted boundary, so two instants in the same UTC day can now compare unequal (and adjacent-day instants equal), silently reclassifying day-boundary/billing-cutoff decisions for any consumer of this exported API.

findings.title: billingDay silently changes from UTC to server-local timezone
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation derived the billing day from UTC fields (getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate @base faa7bb0); the new body uses local-time fields (getFullYear/getMonth/getDate). Output is now environment-dependent: for any process whose TZ is not UTC, billingDay(new Date('2025-06-01T13:30:00Z')) returns '2025-05-31' under TZ=Pacific/Auckland but '2025-06-01' under TZ=UTC — a daily window where the returned day shifts. This (a) makes billing boundaries depend on host locale instead of a fixed calendar, and (b) desynchronizes freshly computed values from any records already keyed/grouped on the old UTC values: sameBillingDay (src/billing/day.ts:7-9) compares strings, so a stored UTC-derived day vs a newly computed local-derived day for the same instant now disagree, misclassifying billing-day boundaries (double or missed billing on rollover). The exported public contract changed with no name change, config knob, or migration — the definitive UTC basis was the prior observable behavior.

findings.title: billingDay silently changes UTC day to host-local day, breaking billing attribution
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation deliberately used getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate; the new code uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, so the returned YYYY-MM-DD now depends on the host's ambient timezone instead of the input Date. Substituted real values: for instant 2024-01-05T23:30:00Z a UTC host yields '2024-01-05' (matching all previously persisted values) while a TZ=Asia/Tokyo host yields '2024-01-06'; for 2024-01-05T00:30:00Z a TZ=America/New_York host yields '2024-01-04'. findings.title: Cache key drops tenant scope, returning wrong tenant's profile
findings.whyItBreaks: `memo` is a module-scoped Map shared by all callers, and readProfile's signature fetches per (tenant, account). With key = account: caller A calls readProfile("t1", "acct", f) — miss, fetches t1's profile, memo.set("acct", t1Profile). Caller B then calls readProfile("t2", "acct", f) — memo.get("acct") hits at line 15 and returns t1's profile (displayName/tenant fields belong to t1) without ever calling fetchProfile. After the first call, the `tenant` argument is silently inert for any account name already cached. Two tenants sharing an account identifier is the ordinary case this two-parameter API exists for; the substitution yields a concrete wrong-data (cross-tenant leak) path on this exported public function.

findings.title: Drop tenant from memo key leaks profiles across tenants
findings.whyItBreaks: `memo` (src/profile.ts:7) is module-global and shared by every `readProfile` call regardless of tenant. findings.title: Cache key omits tenant: cross-tenant profile collision and stale wrong-tenant return

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error into "" — failure indistinguishable from stored empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: The function deliberately throws `Error('missing: ' + key)` (line 4) and the new bare `catch { return ""; }` (lines 6-8) immediately discards it — unlogged and unbound, so it also swallows any other runtime error in the try block. "" is a perfectly valid value in a Map<string,string>, so callers can no longer distinguish 'key missing' from 'key present with empty value'. This is an exported/public API: previously `load` propagated the error to its caller, and `loadAll` (src/store.ts:12) propagated it through its `keys.map` to its caller — a miss was a loud, key-identifiable failure. Now `loadAll(['a','missing','b'], s)` silently returns `['x','','y']`, and any consumer acting on the result (persistence, join/output formatting, validation) treats the miss as real data. No doc or contract declares "" as the not-found convention, so the fallback is not an API contract — it is a swallowed signal shipped in a public path.

findings.title: Public load()/loadAll() now swallow missing-key errors into ""

Both symbols are exported, so this broken contract ships now; any eventual caller is forced to act on the fallback value as real data.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error and returns "", conflating absent key with empty value

findings.title: retryBackground duplicates retry; shared Config requires fields each ignores
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground (lines 20-31) is a line-for-line copy of retry whose only behavioral difference is reading config.retries instead of config.maxAttempts. Both share Config, which now requires maxAttempts, retries AND timeout (lines 2-4), but retry ignores retries and retryBackground ignores maxAttempts. Verified via rg: zero in-repo callers, so the defect is the exported API contract itself.

findings.title: retryBackground swallows all errors; exhaustion indistinguishable from success
findings.whyItBreaks: Newly added public path discards every failure signal: 'catch { continue; }' (lines 27-29) drops the exception without logging or recording it, and after exhausting all retries the function falls out and returns void (line 31) — the same observable outcome as success via the early return at line 26. previously_reached=nothing (function is new; there is no prior propagation point — the error now reaches nothing). Every eventual caller is forced to conflate 'fn succeeded' with 'all attempts failed' and, per TRIGGER D, this unusable contract is a present defect even with zero in-repo callers (verified via rg). A caller that treats the return as success will persist/report work that never happened. Note: retry (line 14) has the same catch shape but it is pre-existing at base 21b417c and unchanged by this diff, so it is not charged here.

findings.title: retryBackground duplicates retry(); shared Config forces dead required fields
findings.whyItBreaks: Lines 20-31 are byte-identical to existing retry() (lines 7-18) except the loop bound reads config.retries instead of config.maxAttempts (proved: diff of the two bodies differs only on lines 1 and 3). findings.title: Deploy secret is echoed into workflow logs; remove the print
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step maps TOKEN: ${{ secrets.TOKEN }} (line 11) and the run at line 12 interpolates it into output: `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`. The env is step-scoped, so nothing downstream consumes it — `make build` (line 13) never sees TOKEN. The secret's only destination is the job log. Shipping an intentional secret-to-log path that serves no purpose is a defect on its own, independent of whether the current masking happens to hold.

findings.title: Deploy step echoes secrets.TOKEN value into workflow logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The new step maps secrets.TOKEN into the run environment and executes `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`, which writes the secret's value into the workflow job log of a workflow that runs on every push (on: push). GitHub's automatic masking of secrets-context values is best-effort exact-string matching: any later transform of $TOKEN (base64, trimming, concatenation, substring), or a short/common-token value, leaks the real secret into logs, which for public repos are readable by anyone. The direct verbatim echo currently renders as ***, so exposure is conditional on masking holding — but intentionally printing a secret is the documented anti-pattern, and a deploy pipeline must not rely on the masker. No in-repo consumer needs the value printed (rg shows TOKEN used nowhere else).

findings.title: Secret value echoed into workflow logs; masking is the only safeguard
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step injects secrets.TOKEN as an env var and then runs `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`, emitting the secret's value into the job log. The workflow triggers `on: push`, so this runs on every push and the log (including the echoed line) is retained and downloadable by anyone with read access to the repo. The only thing preventing disclosure is GitHub Actions' automatic log masking, a runtime best-effort mechanism that is documented-unreliable for multi-line values, transformed/expanded values, and partial matches — it is not a code-level guarantee. The secret is not passed to `make build` or any deploy logic, so the step's entire function is printing the secret; there is no legitimate purpose that justifies the exposure. If the intent is to verify the secret is configured, the check must not emit its value.

findings.title: git() maxBuffer removal caps diff output at 1 MiB default, breaking large-PR reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync without maxBuffer uses Node's default of 1 MiB. git() at line 140 runs `git diff <mergeBase> <headSha>` and returns the entire PR patch; any diff over 1 MiB (lockfiles, generated code, bulk edits) makes the child exceed maxBuffer: it is killed, res.status is null (not 0), and line 38-39 throws `git diff ... failed: ` with truncated/empty stderr. The run then posts a 'Needlefish: review failed' check and sets exit 1 (catch block). Previously this worked up to 64 MiB; the sibling gh()/ghText() helpers keep maxBuffer: 1024*1024*64 (lines 19, 29), so this call site is the one that needed the buffer. Large-diff PRs regress from reviewed to hard-failed.

findings.title: Bundle now reports baseSha but patch/changedFiles are diffed from mergeBase
findings.whyItBreaks: patch (line 140) and changedFiles (line 141, via changedFileSet) are computed against mergeBase (line 139), but the bundle now ships baseSha (line 138) instead of mergeBase. When PR_BASE_SHA is set — the intended Actions path, cf. PR_HEAD_SHA at line 137 — to the base-branch tip, baseSha differs from mergeBase whenever the base branch advanced after the PR branch was cut (a routine occurrence: another PR merged to main). The bundle then contains mutually inconsistent inputs: a patch/change-list covering mergeBase..head plus a baseSha pointing at a different commit. Any downstream consumer that uses bundle.baseSha to re-diff, read pre-image file content, or anchor inline comments operates on a different base than the patch it is given, yielding phantom/missing changes and misaligned comment lines. (In the PR_BASE_SHA-unset fallback the change is a no-op, so the defect is specific to the primary CI path.)

findings.title: Restore 64 MiB maxBuffer in git() or large PR diffs fail the whole review
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff removes maxBuffer: 1024*1024*64 from the git() spawnSync, falling back to Node's default maxBuffer of 1 MiB (1024*1024). git() is called at line 140 with ["diff", mergeBase, headSha], which streams the entire PR patch — unbounded output that routinely exceeds 1 MiB (lockfiles, generated or vendored files). On overflow, spawnSync kills the child (ENOBUFS) and res.status is null, so line 38 throws with an empty stderr message; runGithub's catch (line ~175) then posts a failed 'Needlefish: review failed' check run and sets exit code 1. PRs whose diff is between 1 MiB and 64 MiB were reviewed before this change and now hard-fail. The regression is also inconsistent with the sibling gh()/ghText() helpers, which still carry the 64 MiB maxBuffer (lines 19, 29).

findings.title: Restore 64 MiB maxBuffer in git(); removal breaks reviews of >1 MiB diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: git() is used for the full PR patch (git ["diff", mergeBase, headSha] at src/adapters/github.ts:140) and the file list (line 57). With maxBuffer removed, Node's spawnSync default of 1024*1024 bytes applies; a diff larger than 1 MiB causes Node to kill the git child (status=null), so `res.status !== 0` at line 38 throws and runGithub's catch posts a failing 'Needlefish: review failed' check with exit code 1. The sibling helpers gh() (line 19) and ghText() (line 29) retain the 64 MiB cap, confirming the removal is inconsistent with the file's own remaining code and regresses large-PR review.

findings.title: Restore explicit read-only sandbox for codex exec agent runs
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex spawns the Codex agent with cwd set to an arbitrary target repo and feeds it a prompt derived from that repo's untrusted content, returning only the agent's last message. The removed '-s read-only' flag was the only mechanism pinning the agent to a non-mutating sandbox; the CLI flag overrides ambient config. With the flag gone, Codex resolves sandbox mode from ~/.codex/config.toml (or project config), so on any machine configured with sandbox_mode=workspace-write or danger-full-access, a prompt-injected agent can now modify or destroy files in the repo under review (or run arbitrary commands in full-access mode), whereas before this change the spawn was forced read-only regardless of environment. This is a silent weakening of a security control on an agent-execution path over untrusted input; no other flag, env var, or config in the file constrains the agent.

findings.title: Restore enforced read-only sandbox on spawned codex exec
findings.whyItBreaks: The only change in this PR deletes ["-s", "read-only"] from the argv. With the flag gone, the spawned `codex exec` no longer forces sandbox mode: it falls back to the ambient Codex config (~/.codex/config.toml, profiles) or the CLI default. Configs using the common 'full-auto' setup set sandbox_mode=workspace-write (or danger-full-access), and `codex exec` is non-interactive, so approval prompts cannot gate anything. runCodex runs the agent with cwd=opts.repoPath (src/shared/codex.ts:27-33), so under such a config model-generated commands can now modify the target repo and reach the network, where the previous line guaranteed read-only regardless of local config. Nothing in the file or repo compensates: there is no --sandbox, no approval flag, no env scrubbing (verified by reading the full file and rg over the repo).

findings.title: Remove `-s read-only`: codex exec loses its pinned read-only sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex spawns `codex exec` with cwd=opts.repoPath and stdin=prompt, and is the shared helper for driving codex over repository content that is attacker-influenced (reviewed PR diffs). The base code pinned the sandbox to `read-only`, guaranteeing the subprocess could not write files regardless of environment. Removing `-s read-only` makes the effective sandbox resolve from codex's ambient config/default (`~/.codex/config.toml` sandbox_mode or CLI defaults), which this function neither sets nor can see. Substituted effect: on any machine configured with `sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"` or `"danger-full-access"`, the spawned agent can now mutate the repository under review (or the host) — e.g. via prompt injection embedded in the diff being reviewed — where previously every write was blocked. Under default configs the behavior is unchanged, which is exactly why this weakening is silent: nothing in the code or output distinguishes the permissive run from the pinned one. A pinned least-privilege flag on a public exported path (src/shared) handling untrusted input is a security boundary; removing it is a regression even though nothing in-repo calls runCodex yet.

findings.title: Diff uses raw PR_BASE_SHA instead of merge-base, polluting review with base-branch changes
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed `merge-base(baseSha, headSha)` call normalized PR_BASE_SHA (which GitHub reports as the base-branch tip, not the PR's fork point) to the true common ancestor. Now, whenever the base branch has advanced past the PR's fork point (normal for any PR open for hours, and guaranteed if main advances between event time and workflow run), `git diff baseSha HEAD` returns the PR's changes PLUS reversed hunks of unrelated main-side commits, and changedFileSet lists files the PR never touched. Consequences in this same file: review(bundle) at line 176 receives a polluted patch and can request changes on code the author never wrote; inlineComments (lines 61-69) filters findings only by changedPaths membership, so inline comments can be posted on the PR for lines the PR did not modify. Additionally, the right side changed from headSha (honoring PR_HEAD_SHA) to literal HEAD: under Actions' default pull_request checkout (merge ref refs/pull/N/merge), the diff is computed against the local merge commit while postReview posts commit_id: headSha (line 178) and postCheck posts head_sha: headSha (line 179) — review content and the commit it is anchored to diverge. The no-env local path is unaffected (baseSha is already the merge-base, so old and new coincide).

findings.title: Dropped merge-base normalization corrupts patch when PR_BASE_SHA is not an ancestor
findings.whyItBreaks: PR_BASE_SHA is a supported input (line 138). When it is set to a base-branch tip that has advanced past the fork point (e.g. github.event.pull_request.base.sha after new commits land on main), baseSha is not an ancestor of HEAD. The deleted `merge-base baseSha headSha` line normalized the diff base to the fork point so the patch contained only PR changes; the new `git diff baseSha HEAD` (line 139) instead returns PR changes PLUS the reverse of every base-branch-only commit, and changedFileSet(cwd, baseSha) (lines 68-71, `diff --name-only baseSha HEAD`) lists files the PR never touched. The corrupted surface flows into the review bundle (patch/changedFiles) and changedPaths, so inlineComments (line 105) can target files outside the PR diff and the GitHub review POST fails or reviews changes the PR did not make. Additionally the head side changed from headSha to literal "HEAD": with PR_HEAD_SHA set to a commit that is not checked out, the reviewed diff no longer matches the commit_id the review/check-run is attributed to (lines 166, 193). The default no-env path is unaffected (merge-base(baseSha, headSha) == baseSha there).

findings.title: Diff now computed against checkout HEAD but attributed to PR_HEAD_SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff source changed from merge-base(baseSha, headSha)..headSha to baseSha..HEAD, while headSha (process.env.PR_HEAD_SHA || rev-parse HEAD, line 137) is still what results are attached to: commit_id in the review payload (line 85), head_sha in check runs (line 124), bundle.headSha (line 165). Whenever PR_HEAD_SHA is set and the checkout HEAD is not the PR head — the only reason this env var exists, e.g. an Actions refs/pull/N/merge checkout — (a) patch and changedFiles describe the checkout's delta, not the PR head's, so the pass/REQUEST_CHANGES verdict is driven by changes the PR does not contain; (b) inline comments carry side:RIGHT line numbers taken from the HEAD diff, which GitHub validates against commit_id=headSha and rejects (422), silently degrading through the postReview catch (line 96) to a body-only review with no inline comments. Additionally, when PR_BASE_SHA is set to the base branch tip and the base branch has advanced since the fork, git diff baseSha HEAD presents other merged PRs' changes in reverse as part of this patch, and changedFileSet/changedPaths (line 63 filter) include files the PR never touched, inflating and misattributing the review surface. Old code normalized both cases via merge-base(baseSha, headSha). When the env vars are unset the change is a no-op (baseSha is already an ancestor of HEAD and headSha==HEAD); the defect is precisely on the env-var paths the code reads first.

findings.title: Removed merge-base call silently drops headSha validation (fail-loud → fail-silent)
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER D. The removed `git merge-base baseSha headSha` was the only point that validated that the requested head commit resolves in the local clone and shares ancestry with the base; on failure it threw, reached the catch at line 181, and published a 'Needlefish: review failed' failure check plus exit 1 — an explicit, observable error signal. After this change the same condition produces no signal at all: the run reviews the checkout's patch and publishes a normal pass/changes_requested verdict and check run against head_sha=PR_HEAD_SHA (line 124) even though that commit's content was never diffed. The consumer of the check run (branch protection) cannot distinguish 'PR content reviewed and passed' from 'some other content reviewed, PR head unvalidated' — failure is now indistinguishable from a legitimate pass.

findings.title: Function replacers removed: `$&`/`$$`/`$'` in bundle text corrupt prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace interprets special patterns in a string replacement per ECMA-262 GetSubstitution: `$$`→`$`, `$&`→the matched placeholder (`{{BUNDLE}}`/`{{FINDINGS}}`/`{{PATCH}}`), `` $` ``→text before the match, `$'`→text after the match. The base code used function replacers exactly to bypass this. The diff reverts to plain string replacements, so any `$&`, `$$`, `$'` or `` $` `` sequence inside JSON.stringify(bundle), JSON.stringify(candidate) or bundle.patch — all free-text derived from the PR under review, where such sequences are common (shell `$$`, sed/perl `$&`, bash `$'...'` quoting) — is silently rewritten. The model then receives a corrupted prompt (e.g. a patch line `sed 's/x/y$&/'` renders as `sed 's/x/y{{PATCH}}/'`), degrading or invalidating the review with no error raised.

findings.title: String-form replace mangles $ patterns in bundle/patch into prompts
findings.whyItBreaks:
String.prototype.replace with a string replacement interprets substitution patterns: $$→$, $&→the matched placeholder, $`→preceding template text, $'→following template text. The old code wrapped each replacement in a function precisely to bypass this; this diff removes that protection on all three sites. Verified by direct stdlib substitution: template 'BEFORE
{{PATCH}}
AFTER' with patch text 'echo $$
sed s/x/$&/
case $'x'' now produces 'echo $
sed s/x/{{PATCH}}/
case 
AFTERx' in esac
AFTER' — the patch is corrupted, the placeholder is re-injected mid-patch, and template text is spliced into the data. bundle.patch (line 33) is raw un-escaped diff text where $$ (Makefile recipes, shell PIDs), $& (sed replacements), and $' (bash ANSI-C quoting) are routine; JSON.stringify output (lines 25, 32) does not escape $ either. The review and critic models then receive corrupted bundles/patches, so verdicts and findings are derived from wrong data — a silent regression on the core path.

findings.title: String replacers corrupt prompts containing $&, $`, $' or $$
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace with a string replacement interprets special patterns in the replacement value: $$ → $, $& → the matched placeholder, $` → everything before the placeholder, $' → everything after it. The base commit wrapped each replacement value in a function specifically to disable this. This diff passes the values as plain strings: JSON.stringify(bundle) (line 25), JSON.stringify(candidate) (line 32), and raw bundle.patch (line 33). JSON.stringify does not escape '$', and patches routinely contain Makefile '$$', bash ANSI-C quoting $'…', and sed 's/x/$&/'. Substituted live: patch "sed s/x/$&/ ; echo $'done' ; make $$VAR" becomes "sed s/x/{{PATCH}}/ ; echo  PROMPT-FOOTERdone' ; make $VAR PROMPT-FOOTER" — placeholder text injected into the patch, the prompt footer duplicated mid-patch, and '$$' silently collapsed. The LLM at runCodex (lines 28/34) reviews corrupted input with no error raised, so verdicts and findings for such patches are silently wrong. The function-replacer form restores exact output.

findings.title: Restore commit_id in fallback review POST (required for COMMENT/REQUEST_CHANGES)
findings.whyItBreaks: The fallback POST fires whenever the primary JSON POST fails (catch at github.ts:100), e.g. a 422 from an inline comment whose lineStart is outside the diff hunks — inlineComments (github.ts:66-77) only filters on path membership and lineStart > 0. VERDICT_EVENT (github.ts:47-52) maps every verdict to 'COMMENT' or 'REQUEST_CHANGES', never 'APPROVE'. The GitHub REST contract for POST repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{n}/reviews documents commit_id as 'required when using REQUEST_CHANGES or COMMENT for the event parameter' — which is why the primary payload still sends commit_id (github.ts:89). After this change the fallback omits it, so gh() throws on the 422 (github.ts:21-23); nothing wraps the fallback call, so the error escapes postReview into runGithub's catch (github.ts:186-196): the check run is posted as conclusion 'failure' titled 'Needlefish: review failed' even for a pass verdict, the review body is never posted, and process.exitCode becomes 1. Before this diff the fallback carried the valid pinned headSha and recovered the review. Secondary effect (if enforcement were lax): the review attaches to whatever the current head is instead of the analyzed commit, inconsistent with the primary path's pinning.

findings.title: normalizeFinding silently fabricates values for malformed findings
findings.whyItBreaks: Base threw on invalid severity/category, missing/empty file-title-whyItBreaks-suggestedFix, and non-finite/<=0 lineStart/lineEnd (base lines 96-125). Head replaces every throw with a default: substitution normalizeFinding({severity:'critical', file:42, lineStart:'12a'}) — base: throws 'malformed finding: invalid severity' — head: returns {severity:'P1', category:'bug', file:'42', lineStart:NaN, lineEnd:NaN, ...}. Failure is now indistinguishable from a genuine finding: invalid severity is masked as the alarming, plausible 'P1' (line 98); non-string file coerced via String() so 42 becomes the bogus path '42' (line 103); lineStart NaN (Number('12a')), negative (-5) and 0 all pass unguarded (line 104); whitespace-only title/file/whyItBreaks pass untrimmed; titles are silently truncated at 120 chars (line 99). normalizeReview (line 131) maps every element through this, so any downstream consumer of RawReview receives fabricated, structurally valid findings and cannot tell failed normalization from real review output — this module's sole purpose is guarding that boundary.

findings.title: normalizeReview drops exported strict param — breaking API change
findings.whyItBreaks: Base exported normalizeReview(raw, strict = true): strict (default) threw on any malformed finding; strict=false dropped them via try/catch filter. Head removes the parameter entirely: any TypeScript caller passing the second argument now fails to compile (Expected 1 arguments, but got 2), and the lenient mode's semantics silently invert from 'drop malformed findings' to 'keep fabricated findings', since normalizeFinding can no longer throw and the drop path (base lines 133-143) is unreconstructable. This is an exported public signature change in a src/shared/ module with no compat shim.

findings.title: normalizeFinding silently fabricates findings from malformed input
findings.whyItBreaks: The validation gate for review output was removed. Base (089c1c2:src/shared/schema.ts:96-122) threw 'malformed finding: ...' on invalid severity/category, empty file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, and non-finite/<=0 lineStart/lineEnd; non-strict mode (base:157-165) dropped such findings. Now: invalid/missing severity becomes "P1" (:98), invalid category becomes "bug" (:100-102), missing file becomes "" (:103), lineStart/lineEnd become 0, NaN, or negative with no finite/positive check (:104-105), and empty whyItBreaks/suggestedFix pass (:107-108). normalizeReview additionally lost the 'strict' parameter (:113) and the drop-invalid filter (raw.findings.map(normalizeFinding) @131 passes everything through), so any existing strict=false caller silently changes from drop-invalid to keep-fabricated. Substitution: normalizeFinding({}) returns {severity:'P1', title:'Untitled finding', category:'bug', file:'', lineStart:0, lineEnd:0, ...} — type-identical to a genuine Finding, so no caller (verdict computation, PR comment rendering) can distinguish model-produced garbage relabeled P1 from a real high-priority finding; garbage is inflated to high severity instead of failing loudly. This is an exported swallow site (TRIGGER D): the public contract itself forces every eventual caller to conflate failure with a valid value.

findings.title: normalizeFinding now launders malformed findings into fabricated P1 defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported validator previously threw 'malformed finding: ...' on invalid severity/category, empty file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, or non-finite line numbers (base lines 96-122). This diff deletes all seven throws and substitutes defaults: invalid severity -> 'P1' (head:98) so unparseable model output like severity 'critical' is ESCALATED to the most alarming valid severity and can flip a downstream review to blocking; empty file -> '' and lineStart -> 0 (head:103-105), which violates Finding's own non-empty/positive contract and is unusable for comment anchoring; and because the old Number.isFinite guards are gone, lineStart:'abc' now persists as NaN. Callers can no longer distinguish a failed parse from a real finding — failure is persisted/reported as a legitimate P1 'bug' finding (TRIGGER D on a public path).

findings.title: normalizeReview drops strict param, losing fail-loud and filter contracts
findings.whyItBreaks: Exported normalizeReview(raw, strict = true) carried two contracts via its signature (base:137): strict (the default) propagated a thrown error on any malformed finding so the pipeline could reject/retry bad model output, and strict=false filtered malformed findings out (base:158-165). This diff removes the parameter — TypeScript callers passing false no longer compile (breaking API change) — and hardcodes raw.findings.map(normalizeFinding) (head:131), which can no longer reject any field-level garbage. The fail-loud error signal is gone (TRIGGER D) and the tolerance path silently changed from 'drop bad findings' to 'launder bad findings into P1/bug defaults' (TRIGGER C: the carrier promised strictness; the body implements none).

findings.title: Restore -R "$REPO": gh pr view can't resolve repo before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The 'Resolve PR refs' step is the first job step (lines 26-40); actions/checkout only runs afterwards (line 42), so the runner workspace has no .git when these gh calls execute. gh resolves the repository solely from -R, the GH_REPO env var, or a git remote in cwd — it never reads Actions' GITHUB_REPOSITORY, and this workflow sets no GH_REPO (verified across the file). The else-branch is the only path for workflow_dispatch (EVENT_HEAD empty on dispatch events), so on a manual dispatch of pr_number: on a fresh/ephemeral workspace or first run, gh fails with 'could not determine which repository to use'; on a warm self-hosted workspace it silently depends on a stale .git left by a previous run's checkout — ambient runner state the workflow no longer controls. Because the failing gh runs inside `echo "head=$(...)"`, bash -eo pipefail masks the command-substitution failure: the step 'succeeds' with empty head/base, actions/checkout (ref: '') falls back to the default branch, and the review runs with PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA empty instead of failing loudly.

findings.title: Drop -R breaks gh repo resolution: empty refs silently reviewed
findings.whyItBreaks: The 'Resolve PR refs' step (line 26) runs BEFORE the first checkout (line 42). On workflow_dispatch (EVENT_HEAD empty), it now calls `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"` with no `-R`. gh resolves the target repository only from the `-R` flag, the `GH_REPO` env var, or git remotes of the CWD — it ignores the `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` var Actions exports, and no `GH_REPO` is set anywhere in this workflow (verified: only occurrence of `github.repository` is the job-level `if` at line 24). On a fresh/ephemeral runner workspace (or any workspace without a leftover `.git` from a prior run — self-hosted reuse is accidental, not guaranteed), `gh` exits non-zero with 'could not determine current repository'. Because the call sits inside `echo "head=$(...)"` under the default `bash -e -o pipefail`, the failure does NOT fail the step: empty `head=` and `base=` are written to GITHUB_OUTPUT. Downstream, `actions/checkout@v4` with `ref: ''` (line 45) falls back to the event ref — the default branch head, not the PR head — and the review step receives empty PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA (lines 56-57). The documented manual trigger (input description: 'manual trigger; bypasses pull_request webhook') thus fails silently or reviews/posts against the wrong commit. The pull_request path is unaffected (line 34 short-circuits), which is exactly why this survives casual testing after a prior run left a checkout behind.

findings.title: gh pr view without -R cannot resolve repo in pre-checkout step; dispatch path breaks
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed lines execute only when EVENT_HEAD is empty, i.e. workflow_dispatch runs (github.event.pull_request is empty for dispatch; the trigger is deliberate per the input description 'manual trigger; bypasses pull_request webhook'). 'Resolve PR refs' is the job's FIRST step (lines 25-40); no actions/checkout or GH_REPO export precedes it. `gh pr view` without -R resolves the repo via the GH_REPO env var (the Actions runner exports GITHUB_REPOSITORY, which gh does not read) or via git remotes in the current working directory — absent here, so gh fails with 'could not determine current repository'. Worse, the step's default `bash -e` does not abort on a failed command substitution inside echo's argument: echo succeeds with an empty value, `head=`/`base=` are written empty, and the step reports success. Downstream, `actions/checkout` with `ref: ''` checks out the default branch instead of the PR head (line 45), so the review runs against the wrong tree with empty PR_HEAD_SHA/PR_BASE_SHA — a silent wrong-target review. On a persistent self-hosted runner the call only works by accident of leftover .git state from a previous job, and in shared-runner setups can resolve a stale remote pointing at a different repository.

findings.title: normalizeReview silently maps malformed output to a passing empty review
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes all five throwing guards ('malformed review output: not an object / summary missing / findings missing / checked missing / residual_risks missing', previously at base lines 116-129) and replaces each failure path with a default: summary -> "" (line 125), findings -> [] (117), checked -> [] (127), residual_risks -> [] (123). normalizeReview is exported from a shared module and parses LLM review output; a truncated or garbage model response (null root, non-array findings, missing summary) now returns RawReview{summary:"", findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]} — byte-for-byte the shape of a legitimate clean review, since a review with zero findings and zero residual_risks (blocks=false) is exactly what a PASS looks like in this schema (Verdict = pass|changes_requested|needs_human, lines 20/68-73). Callers can no longer distinguish 'model output was malformed' from 'review genuinely found nothing', and dropped residual_risks default to non-blocking, so a review that should block becomes a pass. The error signal that previously reached the caller as a thrown Error is now swallowed entirely — not logged, not flagged, not distinguishable at any decision point.

findings.title: normalizeReview replaces malformed-input throws with silent empty-review defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version threw 'malformed review output: ...' for non-object raw, non-string summary, and non-array findings/checked/residual_risks, so a caller could distinguish 'review generation failed / model emitted garbage' from a real result. The head version swallows all five signals: normalizeReview(null), normalizeReview("garbage"), and normalizeReview({}) all return {summary:"", findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]} — byte-for-byte the shape of a legitimate empty review with zero findings and zero blocking residual risks. This is an exported function (public contract of src/shared/schema.ts), so every caller is forced to conflate failure with a valid value: downstream consumers (per the module's own Verdict/ReviewResult types, an aggregator computing pass/changes_requested) will read garbage model output as a clean pass with nothing to retry and no error logged. Previously_reached=src/shared/schema.ts:115-131 (base, the five throw sites); now_receives=an indistinguishable empty RawReview.

findings.title: normalizeReview silently converts malformed review output into an empty pass review
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes all five malformed-output guards (base lines 115-131 threw 'malformed review output: ...') and substitutes defaults. normalizeReview(null), normalizeReview({}) or input whose 'findings' is missing now returns a structurally valid RawReview {summary:"", findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]} — byte-identical in shape to a genuine review that found no issues. The downstream result contract (ReviewResult.verdict, src/shared/schema.ts:75-76) has no failure channel, so any caller deriving a verdict (e.g. findings.length===0 && !residual_risks.some(r=>r.blocks) => 'pass') records a failed/malformed review run as a clean pass. Additionally, a non-string summary (e.g. an object) is coerced via String() to '[object Object]' at line 125 instead of failing, so garbage output is persisted as a real summary. As an exported function this swallow site is a present contract defect: every caller is forced to conflate 'review failed to produce output' with 'review passed'.

findings.title: workflow_dispatch reviews now run on wrong checkout with empty base/head SHAs
findings.whyItBreaks: The job guard (line 24) still admits workflow_dispatch, and the run command (line 47) still falls back to inputs.pr_number, so the dispatch trigger is intentionally live. But on a workflow_dispatch event github.event.pull_request does not exist, so: (1) line 29 ref expression falls back to github.ref — the dispatched branch (typically main) is checked out instead of the PR head, contradicting the file's own self-review contract that 'the PR checkout's own src/ is the tool'; a manually triggered review of PR N now runs main's tool on main's tree. (2) Lines 45-46 set PR_BASE_SHA='' and PR_HEAD_SHA='' and pass them to src/cli.ts (line 47), which previously received API-resolved values from the deleted 'Resolve PR refs' step (old file, base 54c4a2a: gh pr view $PR_NUM --json headRefOid/baseRefOid). The deleted step's if [ -n "$EVENT_HEAD" ] else-branch existed exactly for this event shape. Depending on the CLI, the run either fails on empty SHAs or silently diffs nothing — either way the documented dispatch trigger ('manual trigger; bypasses pull_request webhook') is broken. The pull_request path is value-identical old→new (head.sha, base.sha, base.ref) and unaffected.

findings.title: workflow_dispatch path now checks out wrong ref and passes empty PR SHAs
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow still triggers on workflow_dispatch (lines 10-14, input described as 'manual trigger; bypasses pull_request webhook', admitted by the job if at line 24), but the removed 'Resolve PR refs' step was the only code that handled that event: on workflow_dispatch github.event.pull_request is null, so github.event.pull_request.head.sha evaluates to ''. Substituting: line 29 becomes ref: github.ref — actions/checkout now lands on the branch the dispatch was run against (default-branch tip), not the PR head; per the file's own comment (lines 3-4, 'the PR checkout's own src/ is the tool') the tool reviews the checked-out tree, so a manual dispatch for PR N reviews the wrong revision and posts it as a PR review with pull-requests: write (line 18). Lines 45-46 similarly pass empty PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA to src/cli.ts where the old flow supplied gh-pr-view-resolved SHAs; at minimum the documented dispatch feature regresses from reviewing the PR to reviewing the default branch (or failing in cli.ts on empty SHAs). The pull_request (same-repo) path is unchanged, but the dispatch path this PR explicitly documents as its manual-entry point is broken.

findings.title: workflow_dispatch reviews default branch with empty PR SHAs
findings.whyItBreaks: workflow_dispatch is a declared trigger (on: lines 10-14, required pr_number input) and is explicitly admitted by the job if (line 24), but a workflow_dispatch event carries no github.event.pull_request context. Substituting on that path: checkout ref `github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.ref` (line 29) resolves to github.ref = the branch dispatched on (e.g. main), not the PR head; PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA (lines 45-46) become empty strings; BASE_REF falls back to hardcoded 'main' (line 35) even for PRs targeting other branches. The deleted 'Resolve PR refs' step (base 45ba2f3 review.yml lines 26-49) existed exactly for this case: its else-branch ran `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"` to resolve head/base/base_ref, and 'Checkout PR head' used the resolved head so the PR's own src/ was the tool (self-review mode per the comment at lines 3-5) and pnpm install ran against the PR lockfile. Now a dispatched review runs the default branch's reviewer code against a wrong/undefined diff: it either fails loudly on empty SHAs or posts a review computed from the wrong head/base — silently wrong in the worst case.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer in git(): default 1 MiB aborts reviews of diffs >1 MiB
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff drops `maxBuffer: 1024*1024*64` from spawnSync in git(), so Node's default maxBuffer (1 MiB) now applies. The core payload call `git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"])` at src/adapters/local.ts:100 streams the entire PR diff through this helper. Substitution: for any PR diff >1 MiB, spawnSync overflows the buffer, kills the child (SIGTERM), sets res.error=ENOBUFS, returns status=null with truncated stdout — the guard `res.status !== 0` at line 12 then throws `git diff <sha> HEAD failed:` and runLocal rejects before review(bundle) runs. Every large-diff PR becomes unreviewable via the local adapter. The unchanged gh() helper (line 36) still sets the 64 MiB buffer, so the file's own convention for large outputs shows this removal is inconsistent. The other git() callers (symbolic-ref, config --get, merge-base, rev-parse, diff --name-only) have tiny outputs and are unaffected, but the diff capture is the primary path.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer in git(): 1MiB default breaks large diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff removes `maxBuffer: 1024 * 1024 * 64` from the spawnSync options in git() (src/adapters/local.ts:11), leaving Node's default maxBuffer of 1MiB. git() is called at src/adapters/local.ts:100 with `git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"])` to fetch the full PR patch, with no size bound upstream. When stdout exceeds maxBuffer, spawnSync terminates the child, truncates output, sets res.error (ENOBUFS), and res.status becomes null. The existing check `res.status !== 0` then throws `git diff <base> <head> failed: ` with an empty stderr (the actual cause, res.error, is never read), aborting the entire review. Any legitimate PR with a >1MiB diff (lockfile churn, vendored or generated files) previously worked up to 64MiB and now fails — a regression on the tool's core path. The sibling gh() helper at src/adapters/local.ts:36 keeps its 64MiB maxBuffer, confirming large payloads are an anticipated input class this codebase deliberately sized for.

findings.title: Remove maxBuffer: git diff >1 MiB now kills the review with an empty error
findings.whyItBreaks: Node's spawnSync default maxBuffer is 1 MiB. The changed git() helper is used at src/adapters/local.ts:100 to capture the FULL patch (`git diff <base> <head>`) into the review bundle. For any diff whose output exceeds 1 MiB (~20k changed lines, common for lockfiles, generated code, or vendored files), spawnSync kills the child, sets status=null with error ENOBUFS and empty stderr; the guard at line 12 then throws `git diff <sha> <sha> failed: ` with an empty reason. Previously this worked up to 64 MiB. The inconsistency proves intent: the unchanged gh() helper at lines 33-37 still passes maxBuffer: 1024*1024*64 for pr view output, so large-payload support was deliberately configured and is now silently dropped only on the git side, which handles the largest output of all. This is a user-facing regression on the core review path; failure still throws (no silent data corruption), but large PRs become unreviewable with a misleading empty error message.

findings.title: Review-error check run no longer fails: 'failure' downgraded to 'neutral'
findings.whyItBreaks: postCheck creates the 'Needlefish' check run (name at github.ts:123) that repos use as a required status check. On a review error this now posts conclusion 'neutral' instead of 'failure'. GitHub treats a neutral check run as non-failing for branch protection, so an errored review (gh/api/model failure) no longer blocks merge — the gate fails open. It also makes an errored review indistinguishable from a successful needs_human review, which maps to 'neutral' (github.ts:53), and the summary text in the same call still promises the opposite: 'Review errored and did NOT pass this PR'. Previously the failure signal reached branch protection via conclusion 'failure'; that consumer now receives neutral and allows merge.

findings.title: Review-error check run downgraded from failure to neutral (fail-open gate)
findings.whyItBreaks: In the catch path, postCheck now posts conclusion "neutral" instead of "failure" for the 'Needlefish' check run. A neutral check run does not fail the PR: GitHub treats neutral conclusions as satisfying a required status check, so on any review crash (gh API error, JSON.parse failure in gh(), git failure in changedFileSet, review() throw) the PR becomes mergeable without a completed review. The same payload still asserts 'Review errored and did NOT pass this PR.' (line 193) while its conclusion is treated as passing for merge gating. Failure is also now conclusion-indistinguishable from the completed needs_human verdict (VERDICT_CONCLUSION maps needs_human → neutral, line 53). The old behavior (conclusion "failure") blocked required checks on reviewer crash; this is a fail-open regression on the error path of the tool whose purpose is to gate merges.

findings.title: Review-error check conclusion downgraded to 'neutral', hiding the failure
findings.whyItBreaks: In the catch path, postCheck is now called with conclusion 'neutral' (was 'failure'). 'neutral' is byte-identical to the needs_human verdict conclusion (src/adapters/github.ts:53), so every consumer of the machine-readable 'Needlefish' check conclusion — branch-protection UIs, gh pr checks, alerting that keys on failure — can no longer distinguish 'review errored' from 'needs human'; errored reviews no longer surface as failing checks. The unchanged summary text still asserts 'Review errored and did NOT pass this PR', so the non-failing conclusion now contradicts the message carried in the same payload.

findings.title: Review tool now comes from the PR head; PR can control its own review
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted steps checked the tool out of frankekn/needlefish@main precisely so 'a PR [cannot] control its own review by modifying the tool' (old comment, lines 3-6). This diff deletes that checkout and runs ./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts (line 59) plus 'pnpm install --frozen-lockfile' (line 49) directly in the PR-head checkout. A branch PR can therefore (a) edit src/cli.ts to always emit a passing verdict, defeating the review gate this workflow exists to enforce — the exact attack the removed comment documented; and (b) ship a package.json/pnpm-lock.yaml with pnpm.onlyBuiltDependencies allowlisting malicious postinstall scripts, giving arbitrary code execution at the Install step. That code runs with GH_TOKEN under permissions pull-requests: write / checks: write (lines 17-20) on runs-on: self-hosted (line 23), a persistent runner where untrusted, PR-controlled execution is unsafe. The job-level if (line 25) limits this to same-repo PRs, so the exposed actor is any user who can push a branch — exactly the population the review gate governs, each of whom can now self-approve.

findings.title: PR head code is now executed as the reviewer, enabling self-approving PRs
findings.whyItBreaks: The base revision enforced a trusted-tool split: the reviewer was checked out from frankekn/needlefish@main, pnpm install ran in that trusted dir, and the review executed the trusted tool's cli.ts — the PR head's code was never executed on the runner, which the deleted comment states was to prevent 'a PR from controlling its own review by modifying the tool'. This diff deletes the trusted checkout and instead (a) runs `corepack enable && pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` inside the PR head checkout (line 51), executing PR-controlled dependency install/build scripts, and (b) runs `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` from the PR head (line 59), so any PR that modifies the reviewer executes its own tampered reviewer with GH_TOKEN granted `pull-requests: write` and `checks: write` (lines 16-19, 56) on a self-hosted runner (line 23). A hostile in-repo-branch PR can edit src/cli.ts to post a passing/approving review or green checks on itself, silently defeating the merge gate; it can also run arbitrary code on a persistent self-hosted runner. The unchanged job guard (line 24) restricts this to same-repo branches, but those are exactly the changes this review gate exists to judge, and there is no technical need to run the head's version: the tool from main reviews the base..head diff without executing head code. 'Self-review mode' is intentional, but it removes the security control with no compensation and should not merge.
