findings.title: Severity normalization removed: non-canonical severities silently become P3
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding normalizes untrusted `any` input (sole caller: normalizeReview @src/shared/schema.ts:132, which maps LLM-produced findings). Base code canonicalized first — String(...).trim().toUpperCase() (base schema.ts:96) — so "p0", " P1 ", "p2" all normalized to valid severities and unknown values defaulted to P1. The diff replaces this with a strict `SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity)` check plus a "P3" fallback. Substitution: base returned "P0" for {severity:"p0"}; head returns "P3". Every lowercase/whitespace/non-string variant — an input class the base explicitly defended against — is now silently mapped to the LOWEST severity, and the fallback for missing/unknown also dropped P1→P3. Consumers of RawReview.findings can no longer distinguish a genuine P3 from a malformed P0 (failure-as-value, Trigger D), so critical review findings are buried and severity-driven verdict decisions (e.g. any P0/P1 → changes_requested) can flip to pass. Exported normalizeFinding is a public contract: the name promises normalization the severity body no longer performs (Trigger C).

findings.title: normalizeFinding silently downgrades non-exact severities to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: The base code coerced severity via String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase() before the SEVERITIES check and fell back to "P1". The new code tests raw.severity verbatim and falls back to "P3". normalizeFinding's real input is untyped model output (normalizeReview(raw: any) at src/shared/schema.ts:114 maps raw.findings through it at line 132), where case/whitespace variants are routine. Substitutions: severity="p1" → base "P1" (correct), head "P3" (wrong); severity=" p2 " → base "P2" (correct), head "P3" (wrong); severity="critical" (unknown token) → base "P1" (conservative, stays visible), head "P3" (quietest bucket, silently buried). The consumer normalizeReview publishes these findings as the review's findings (RawReview.findings) where severity drives attention/verdict weighting downstream; failure-to-match and a genuine "P3" are indistinguishable at that point. A P0/P1 finding whose severity string isn't byte-exact is demoted to the least visible severity with no error signal.

findings.title: Severity normalization dropped; invalid/case-variant severities silently become P3
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding's contract (exported, consuming Partial<Finding> via raw:any in normalizeReview) is defensive normalization of untrusted input. Old code computed String(raw.severity ?? '').trim().toUpperCase() before the SEVERITIES check and defaulted misses to P1. New code tests raw.severity raw: input 'p1' now fails SEVERITIES.includes('p1') and falls to the default; input ' P2 ' likewise. Substitution: severity='p1' → includes=false @src/shared/schema.ts:97 → default @99 → P3 (was P1); severity=' P2 ' → P3 (was P2); severity=undefined → P3 (was P1). The caller normalizeReview (src/shared/schema.ts:132) cannot distinguish a silently downgraded finding from a genuine P3, so high-severity findings from case-variant producers are deprioritized without any error signal. Additionally the default itself flipped from fail-high (P1) to fail-silent (P3): unparsable severity output is now mapped to the weakest severity, inverting the fail-safe posture (note category still defaults to 'bug', the attention-grabbing value — the P3 default is inconsistent with it).

findings.title: Restore GitHub token redaction in runCodex child env
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes `const env = {...process.env}` plus the `delete env.GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN/GITHUB_API_TOKEN` lines and drops the `env` option from spawnSync. Node's documented default for spawnSync when `env` is omitted is the parent's full `process.env`, so the `codex exec` child (which runs model-generated shell commands against repo content, including untrusted PR text passed via `input: prompt`) now holds the parent's GitHub credentials in its environment. The read-only sandbox does not prevent reading the env (e.g. `printenv`, `/proc/self/environ`), and any token the model captures can be exfiltrated through the child's output file, which runCodex reads and returns to the caller — a prompt-injection path straight to credential leak. The base code's three targeted `delete`s show this redaction was deliberate defense; this is its silent removal.

findings.title: GitHub tokens now inherited by codex subprocess after sanitizer removal
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex spawns the Codex CLI agent (`codex exec -s read-only`) to execute model-driven work over untrusted repo content. At base, the code built `env = { ...process.env }` and deleted GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, GITHUB_API_TOKEN — proof the authors expected those credentials in the parent environment (e.g. a GitHub Actions PR runner) and deliberately kept them out of the agent subprocess. This diff deletes the sanitizer and the `env` option entirely; per documented Node behavior, child_process.spawnSync then defaults `env` to `process.env`, so the codex process — plus any MCP servers, hooks, or helper binaries it launches, which inherit its environment — now holds the runner's GitHub token. A token that previously could not reach the agent can now be read and used by it (authenticated API calls, commenting, or exfiltration via any tool the agent invokes). The `-s read-only` flag is a CLI-level sandbox this code does not control and does not cover credential visibility in the process environment. Least-privilege regression on a security boundary; no commit message or PR metadata justifies dropping it.

findings.title: GitHub tokens leak to codex child process after env-strip removal
findings.whyItBreaks: The base commit deliberately built `env = {...process.env}` and deleted GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, GITHUB_API_TOKEN before spawning codex, and passed that sanitized env to spawnSync. This diff deletes both the sanitization and the `env` option, so spawnSync falls back to its default: the child inherits the parent's complete environment. Net effect: whenever the parent holds a GitHub credential (always the case on CI runners, where GITHUB_TOKEN/GH_TOKEN are standard), the LLM-driven `codex exec -s read-only` agent now receives a live GitHub token. The agent can read its own environment (printenv/env are reads, permitted in a read-only sandbox) and can echo the token into its output, which runCodex returns to callers and writes to the last-message temp file. If sandbox enforcement is unavailable/falls back, `gh`/`git` commands run by the agent are silently authenticated as the token's identity, so a prompt injection can take authenticated GitHub actions (read private repos, comment, open PRs). The base behavior was an explicit credential-exposure defense; removing it unconditionally re-exposes the credential with no scoping, allowlist, or masking in exchange.

findings.title: Restore fork-PR guard: untrusted PR code now runs on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed line `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the job's only trust gate, restricting the self-hosted `review` job to same-repo PRs. The workflow still triggers on every `pull_request` (opened/synchronize/reopened), which fires for fork PRs. Substituting a fork: head.repo.full_name=`attacker/fork` vs repository — base behavior: job skipped; new behavior: job runs and executes attacker-controlled code on a persistent self-hosted machine: `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` runs the fork's postinstall scripts (line 28) and `tsx src/cli.ts` (line 34) executes the fork's own source with GH_TOKEN injected (lines 32-33). Self-hosted runners are not ephemeral/sandboxed (per GitHub hardening guidance they must never process untrusted PR code): the attacker gains arbitrary code execution on the runner host — persistent state, caches, other jobs' env, network egress, and the runner registration/config on that machine. GitHub's automatic GITHUB_TOKEN read-only downgrade for forks does not mitigate host compromise. No compensating control exists: no `environment:` with required reviewers, no approval step, no other condition anywhere in the file.

findings.title: Restore fork-PR guard: untrusted code now runs on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only trust boundary on a job that runs on a persistent `self-hosted` runner (line 18) and executes PR-supplied code twice: `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 28) runs postinstall scripts of whatever the fork's lockfile pins, and `tsx src/cli.ts` (line 34) runs the fork's own source directly, with `GH_TOKEN` exported into its environment (line 33). After this deletion, any fork PR (trigger is plain `pull_request`, line 8) gains arbitrary code execution on the self-hosted host: persistent compromise, theft of the runner registration token and any credentials in the runner user's env/dotfiles/caches, ability to tamper with future runs, plus the read-scoped GITHUB_TOKEN handed to attacker-controlled code. This is GitHub's documented hard-avoid case (self-hosted runners + untrusted fork PRs).

findings.title: Restore fork guard: deleted same-repo `if` lets fork PRs run code on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` gated the `review` job (runs-on: self-hosted, line 18) to same-repo branches only. With it removed, the workflow — which triggers on `pull_request` [opened, synchronize, reopened] (lines 7-9) — now also runs for PRs from any fork. The job then checks out the fork's head SHA (lines 20-24) and executes fork-controlled code on the self-hosted host: `pnpm install` runs arbitrary postinstall scripts from the fork's dependency tree (lines 26-28) and `tsx src/cli.ts` executes the fork's own source with `GH_TOKEN` in the environment (lines 30-34) under `pull-requests: write` / `checks: write` permissions (lines 11-14). Any external attacker can open a fork PR and get arbitrary code execution on persistent, non-ephemeral runner infrastructure that holds runner registration state and any machine-local credentials, and can pivot (poison caches, hijack the runner, tamper with other PR reviews, post approved-looking reviews via the write-token). GitHub explicitly advises never exposing self-hosted runners to untrusted fork PR workflows. This guard's removal converts the review pipeline itself into the attack vector.

findings.title: Explicit env value 0 now silently becomes the default (5000/2000ms)
findings.whyItBreaks: Precondition substitution on both live consumers: (1) NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS='0' → readRunnerDurationMs @131-135 → base returned 0, so hardKillTimer @117-124 fired SIGKILL on the next tick after SIGTERM ('no grace'); head returns fallbackMs=5000 (@3-6), so the operator's explicit 'kill immediately' silently becomes a 5-second grace. (2) NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS='0' → base returned 0 so giveUpTimer @119-123 force-resolved finish(null,'SIGKILL') immediately; head returns 2000 (@7-9), hanging each timed-out invocation up to 2s extra. Value 0 was fully functional at base (setTimeout(…,0) is valid in Node); this change fixes no defect — it only reinterprets a previously supported setting as 'invalid', conflating explicit-0 with unset and substituting the extreme opposite of the requested behavior, silently, at module load. This breaks old settings on upgrade (config compatibility).

findings.title: Env value 0 for runner kill timers silently falls back to 5000/2000ms defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Substitution performed: with NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0, the old predicate (>= 0) yielded RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0, so at src/shared/runner-process.ts:124 the SIGKILL escalation timer fired immediately after the SIGTERM timeout — a coherent, previously-working "zero grace" setting. The new predicate (> 0) maps 0 to the fallback (5000ms), so the hard kill now fires 5s after SIGTERM instead of immediately; likewise NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 now waits 2000ms before the give-up finish(null,"SIGKILL") at line 123 instead of finishing immediately. The operator's explicit value is discarded with no error or log, and after this change NO env value can express a 0ms escalation delay — the working configuration is silently removed, and each timed-out runner takes up to 7s longer to reap than configured.

findings.title: Restored silent coverage loss: hotspot slice drops changed files with no trace
findings.whyItBreaks: reviewLarge now ends the hotspot list at `sortByRisk(mapResult.hotspots).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)` (line 93, MAX_HOTSPOTS=6) with the coverage backstop deleted. Whenever the map pass returns >6 hotspots, or leaves any changed file unmapped (map is an LLM pass — both cases existed before, which is why the backstop existed), those files are never deep-reviewed: no findings are collected for them (loop 97-106 iterates only selected hotspots), no `[name]` entry lands in checked[], and residual_risks is hardcoded [] (line 113). The deleted comment stated the invariant explicitly: 'never silently skip a changed file'. The returned ReviewResult (lines 123-129) reports a normal verdict while part of the diff was never examined — the tool's core guarantee is broken for exactly the large PRs this path exists for.

findings.title: Deep-pass residual risks (incl. blocks:true) discarded; critic and verdict never see them
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER D (swallowed failure). The deep loop reads only `res.findings` (line 104); `res.residual_risks` — the RawReview field the deep passes produce, including any blocks:true signals — is never read, and candidateMerged hardcodes `residual_risks: []` (line 113). Previously the collected residuals were placed in candidateMerged, serialized into the critic prompt via {{FINDINGS}} (line 116), and flowed through `pruned.residual_risks` into both `deriveVerdict(pruned.findings, pruned.residual_risks)` (line 122) and the public `residualRisks` output (line ~128). Now every deep-stage residual is erased before the critic runs: a deep pass that flags 'X not verified, blocks:true' contributes nothing, deriveVerdict can never gate on it, and the public ReviewResult.residualRisks contract reports an empty list. Failure is no longer distinguishable from 'no residual risk' at any downstream decision point.

findings.title: One failed deep pass now aborts the whole large-PR review
findings.whyItBreaks: The per-hotspot try/catch was removed. `extractJson`/`normalizeReview` throw on malformed LLM output — the file's own error strings at lines 57/64/120 acknowledge this happens in practice — and up to 6 deep passes run per review (lines 97-106). With the old code, a failed pass was isolated: remaining hotspots were still reviewed, '[name] DEEP PASS FAILED: …' was recorded in checked[], and a blocks:true residual was emitted. Now the first throwing pass propagates out of reviewLarge, so the entire review() call rejects and returns nothing — no findings from the passes that succeeded, no partial checked[], no result at all. A single flaky LLM response turns a usable degraded review into total failure of the large-PR workflow.

findings.title: Restore tail-coverage backstop: changed files are now silently skipped in large-PR review
findings.whyItBreaks: reviewLarge now runs `sortByRisk(mapResult.hotspots).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)` and goes straight into the deep loop with no coverage check. Two deterministic skip paths: (1) any file the map pass failed to assign to a hotspot, and (2) ALL files in hotspots 7+ (slice cap MAX_HOTSPOTS=6 — previously rescued because `covered` was computed from the selected hotspots only and a tail hotspot picked up the rest). The deleted comment stated the invariant: 'never silently skip a changed file'. A skipped file produces no finding, no checked[] entry, and no residual risk, so deriveVerdict (line 122) can return a clean verdict for a large PR (>10 files / >30k patch — the entire reviewLarge path) while whole files were never examined.

findings.title: Deep-pass residual_risks are parsed then discarded; critic and verdict see hardcoded []
findings.whyItBreaks: The deep loop (line 103) parses each hotspot's RawReview including residual_risks, but `res.residual_risks` is never read — the removed `residuals.push(...res.residual_risks)` propagation is replaced by the hardcoded literal `residual_risks: []` in candidateMerged (line 113), which is JSON-serialized into the critic prompt (line 116). Previously, deep-phase uncertainty signals (ResidualRisk entries, including blocks:true flags like 'could not verify X') flowed into the critic input and could shape pruned.residual_risks; deriveVerdict(pruned.findings, pruned.residual_risks) at line 122 and the user-facing residualRisks (line 128) therefore no longer see deep-phase blockers. A deep pass that reported blocking uncertainty and one that fully verified are now indistinguishable to the verdict path beyond prose, so the final verdict can be strictly more confident than the evidence supports.

findings.title: Coverage backstop removed: unmapped/overflow changed files silently skipped in large-PR review
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted block (old lines 98-110, comment: 'never silently skip a changed file') guaranteed every changed file was deep-reviewed. Now coverage is solely sortByRisk(mapResult.hotspots).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS) @line 93: files the LLM map fails to assign, plus ALL files of hotspots dropped by slice(0,6), get no deep pass. The result still reports a verdict, and `checked` (line 105) and residualRisks (line 128, now only the critic's output) contain no marker of the skipped files — a defect in a skipped file ships with a clean review. Old behavior caught both classes (covered set computed after the slice); new behavior catches neither.

findings.title: Deep-pass residual_risks discarded; candidateMerged hardcodes residual_risks: []
findings.whyItBreaks: TRIGGER D (propagation branch removed, failure/risk → default empty). Previously res.residual_risks from each deep pass flowed to residuals (old line 127) → candidateMerged.residual_risks (old line 140) → serialized into the critic's {{FINDINGS}} input, the only channel that could carry hotspot-level risk signals (e.g. unreviewable files, missing AGENTS.md) into the final residualRisks (line 128) and deriveVerdict (line 122). Now the loop body reads only res.findings/res.summary; res.residual_risks is never read, and candidateMerged.residual_risks is hardcoded [] @line 113. The critic is shown an explicit 'no residual risks' signal, so deep-pass risks cannot re-enter the result; failure/signal and a genuinely clean review are indistinguishable downstream. This compounds finding 1: silently skipped files are no longer flagged by any mechanism.

findings.title: Caller focus/deep inputs now silently ignored on large-PR path only
findings.whyItBreaks: Head has zero remaining reads of bundle.focus/bundle.deep in reviewLarge (rg confirms): focus/deep are dropped from mapBundle (83-89) and {{FOCUS}} is gone from the deep prompt (117-121), so a caller-supplied focus hint or deep flag is silently ignored — no error, no output notice — for any PR over LARGE_PATCH_CHARS/LARGE_FILE_COUNT. Meanwhile reviewSmall still forwards the whole bundle including focus/deep (line 54 JSON.stringify(bundle)), so the public Bundle inputs behave differently depending on PR size. The Bundle type and callers still pass these fields (untouched by this diff), so this is an incoherent partial removal, not deliberate feature retirement.

findings.title: Deleting {{FOCUS}} substitution leaks raw placeholder into deep.md prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: At base, deepPrompt substituted {{FOCUS}} (deleted line: .replace("{{FOCUS}}", bundle.focus ?? "(none)"), base line 122) — every other replace call here ({{BUNDLE}}, {{AGENTS}}, {{HOTSPOT}}, {{BASE}}, {{HEAD}}, {{FINDINGS}}, {{PATCH}}) exists to fill a placeholder in its template, so prompts/deep.md contains {{FOCUS}}. This PR changes only src/core/review.ts (patchStat: 1 file changed), so deep.md is unchanged and still contains {{FOCUS}} at head. After the deletion, the assembled deepPrompt (review.ts:117-121) is passed unmodified to runCodex at review.ts:124, so every deep pass of every large-PR review sends the literal string '{{FOCUS}}' to the model, and the user's focus input is silently dropped from the large path — while reviewSmall (unchanged) still serializes bundle.focus into review.md, making the same input honored for small PRs and ignored for large ones with no error or signal.

findings.title: formatDuration emits '1m 60s' for durations near a minute boundary
findings.whyItBreaks: Rounding happens after the floor-split: for ms=119999, line 90 gives minutes=1 and line 91 gives seconds=Math.round(59999/1000)=60, so renderMarkdown prints '1m 60s' (render.ts:75/80). The base implementation rounded total seconds first (round(119999/1000)=120 → '2m 0s') and could never produce 60 in the seconds slot; for ms=59999 the new code prints '60s' where the old printed '1m 0s', an inconsistency introduced by this diff.

findings.title: formatDuration can render '1m 60s' for durations just under a minute boundary
findings.whyItBreaks: The new code floors minutes from raw ms (line 90) and rounds the remainder to seconds independently (line 91). Substituting a real elapsed duration ms=119970 (a ~2-minute total landing within the 50ms window [119500,120000)): minutes=floor(119970/60000)=1, seconds=round(59970/1000)=60 → output '1m 60s'. The old code rounded total ms to seconds first (totalSeconds=120 → '2m 0s'), so seconds could never exceed 59. Same defect at ms=59950 → '60s' instead of '1m 0s'. Both call sites (src/shared/render.ts:75 per-call durationMs, :80 totalDurationMs) pass real elapsed timings, so the rendered review summary can emit malformed 'Nm 60s'/'60s' strings.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0 and empty strings, breaking its contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function's name (`parsePositiveInteger`) and its unchanged error text at line 33 ('requires a positive integer') promise values >= 1. Changing the bound from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0` makes the body implement 'non-negative' instead. Concrete substitution: Number('') === 0 and Number.isInteger(0) is true, and 0 < 0 is false, so parsePositiveInteger('', label) — and likewise '0', '   ', '-0' — now returns 0 instead of throwing. Previously these inputs threw at the caller; now the invalid/absent input is silently converted into the valid value 0 and flows into whatever sizing/retry/count arithmetic (cf. RunnerOptions.timeoutMs, RunStat.attempts in the same module) the caller feeds it. This is validation weakening plus failure-mapped-to-default on a public path: every eventual caller is forced to conflate 'invalid input' with a legitimate 0. The bound and the carriers must agree.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0, breaking its name/error contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Substitution with the new guard: parsePositiveInteger('0', X) → Number('0')=0, Number.isInteger(0)=true, 0<0=false → no throw, returns 0. The unchanged carriers still promise ≥1: the exported symbol name `parsePositiveInteger` (line 30) and the error text `${label} requires a positive integer` (line 33, still thrown for -1 while 0 passes). This is an exported validation gate, so the drift directly changes the data a caller receives: any consumer parsing a count/limit/timeout (e.g. attempts, timeoutMs in the same module's RunnerOptions/RunStat) is handed 0 as a valid 'positive' value where the previous release rejected it; downstream arithmetic or loops seeded with 0 (zero retries, zero-length timeout) silently misbehave while the caller trusts the promise. The defect is the unusable contract itself, shipping now — it does not depend on a future caller.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0, breaking its promised contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported carrier `parsePositiveInteger` and its unchanged error text `${label} requires a positive integer` (src/shared/runner.ts:33) promise that non-positive integers are rejected. Substituting real values into the changed guard at src/shared/runner.ts:32: input "0" → Number("0")=0, Number.isInteger(0)=true, 0<0=false → no throw, function returns 0. Worse, input "" and "   " coerce via Number() to 0 and also now pass silently, where the previous `parsed <= 0` guard rejected them. Every eventual caller of this public function receives a success value (0) exactly where the contract promised a thrown validation error — failure and a legitimate value are conflated, and 0 can then flow into sizing/timeout/retry arithmetic as if valid. Because the carrier is exported/public, the promise itself is the contract; no in-repo caller is needed to establish the defect. If accepting 0 was intended, the name and error message were not updated, so the asymmetric change is contract drift, not a deliberate relaxation.
